summary: Describes a protocol that lets a WebNFS client negotiate a security mechanism with a WebNFS server before falling back to the MOUNT version 3 protocol. It is published so others can write compatible software. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Before sharing files, the two computers agree on which lock to use. This explains how they choose.

questions: how does webnfs pick a security mechanism
how does webnfs client negotiate security
subtitle: Protocol for WebNFS clients to negotiate security mechanisms with servers.

tldr.problem: WebNFS clients cannot negotiate which security mechanism to use with a server until they fall back to the MOUNT protocol, which adds an extra step and network latency.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol uses a modified LOOKUP request with a special 0x81 byte prefix to ask the server which security mechanisms it supports. The server embeds the list of supported mechanisms in an overloaded filehandle that normally contains just a file reference.
tldr.outcome: Clients can determine the correct security mechanism with a single LOOKUP request before attempting file access, eliminating the need to fall back to MOUNT just for security negotiation.

today: RFC 2755 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the specification for WebNFS security negotiation in implementations that support this extension.

sections.title: WebNFS and Security
sections.content:
The WebNFS protocol lets clients access files from a server without needing a separate mount step; they can start using a public filehandle right away. However, WebNFS clients do not know in advance which security mechanism (such as encryption strength or authentication method) the server requires for a given path. The MOUNT v3 protocol has a procedure that lists available security mechanisms, but WebNFS clients try to skip MOUNT entirely. This creates a gap: the client needs to know which security mechanisms are valid before it can proceed.

RFC 2755 defines a protocol extension called SNEGO-MCL (Security Negotiation Multi-component LOOKUP) that lets a WebNFS client ask the server for its security options in a single LOOKUP request, the same kind of request the client already sends to fetch files.
sections.plainLanguage: Usually WebNFS skips the step of asking the server what security it needs. This explains how to ask anyway, using the same request the client already sends to get files.

sections.title: How WebNFS Works Today
sections.content:
MOUNT versions 1 and 2 were designed for NFS v2, and they do not support security negotiation. MOUNT v3, used with NFS v3, includes a procedure called MOUNTPROC3_MNT that returns both a filehandle and an array of security mechanisms the server supports for a path. When an NFS client mounts a filesystem, it can see which security mechanisms are available and pick one.

WebNFS, however, assumes the server supports the public filehandle and starts with LOOKUP requests directly. If those fail with an AUTH_TOOWEAK error, the client learns that it needs a stronger security mechanism, but it still has to fall back to the MOUNT protocol to find out which ones are available. The new SNEGO-MCL mechanism avoids this.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular mounting with MOUNT v3 asks the server for security choices first. WebNFS skips that, so this protocol adds it back when needed.

sections.title: The SNEGO-MCL Request and Response
sections.content:
A SNEGO-MCL request is a regular LOOKUP request with a specially formatted pathname. Instead of a path like /export/home, the client sends a path that starts with a 0x81 byte (to signal that security negotiation is requested) followed by a security index byte, then the actual pathname. The security index starts at 1 and increments with each request, allowing the client to fetch multiple batches of security mechanisms if the server supports many of them.

The server responds with what appears to be a filehandle, but it is actually an overloaded filehandle containing an array of supported security mechanisms, each represented as a 4-octet integer. NFS v2 filehandles are 32 octets, so they can hold up to seven mechanisms. NFS v3 filehandles can be up to 64 octets, accommodating up to fifteen mechanisms. If more exist, the server sets a status flag to indicate the client should send another SNEGO-MCL request.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends a LOOKUP with a special marker (0x81) followed by a number asking for the next batch. The server replies with a fake filehandle that actually contains a list of security options, fitting as many as will fit in the space.

sections.title: The Negotiation Flow
sections.content:
The typical flow begins when a WebNFS client attempts a regular LOOKUP for a path using its default security mechanism, typically AUTH_SYS. If the server rejects it with AUTH_TOOWEAK, the client knows the default is not strong enough. Instead of giving up, the client sends a SNEGO-MCL request using the same default security mechanism. The server, understanding the 0x81 prefix, responds with the list of available security mechanisms in the overloaded filehandle.

The client examines this list, picks the first mechanism it also supports (the order reflects the server's preference), and issues a new LOOKUP request using that mechanism to get the real filehandle for the path. All subsequent NFS operations then use the selected mechanism and filehandle. If the server does not support WebNFS security negotiation, the SNEGO-MCL request fails with NFSERR_IO (for NFS v2) or NFS3ERR_IO (for NFS v3), signaling to the client that it should fall back to MOUNT v3.
sections.plainLanguage: The client tries with its default security and gets rejected. It then asks for a list of options using the same default. Once it has the list, it picks the best one and tries again with that choice.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The protocol is designed to be backward compatible with servers that do not implement security negotiation. When a server does not recognize the 0x81 prefix as a signal for security negotiation, it treats the request as a malformed path and returns an error. The client, recognizing this error code, knows the server does not support SNEGO-MCL and falls back to attempting MOUNT v3 if needed. Servers that do implement it simply check for the 0x81 byte and respond with the overloaded filehandle when present.

The protocol also minimizes network round trips by allowing the client to request multiple batches of mechanisms in a single exchange without waiting for a response before preparing the next request. This is critical for applications where network latency is a significant cost.
sections.plainLanguage: If the server does not understand the special 0x81 marker, it sends back an error, and the client knows to try the old way. Servers that do understand it just send the list.
